question_text: Your effective batch size is 256 but a single batch of that size doesn't fit in GPU memory. How does gradient accumulation help, and what's the catch?
model_answer:
Gradient accumulation simulates a large batch by running multiple smaller forward-backward passes and summing gradients before stepping the optimizer. If memory holds 64 samples, you do 4 micro-batches of 64, accumulate gradients across them, then take one optimizer step as if you had a 256-sized batch. ```python
optimizer.zero_grad()
for i, batch in enumerate(loader):
    loss = model(batch) / accum_steps  # scale to keep gradient magnitude correct
    loss.backward()
    if (i + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
```
The catch is that gradient accumulation is only mathematically equivalent to a larger batch for the gradient itself, not for everything else. Specifically: BatchNorm computes statistics per micro-batch, so accumulating 4 micro-batches of 64 gives you 4 separate normalization regimes, not one over 256. With BN, accumulation doesn't actually replicate the larger-batch behavior, which is why models that depend on BN often need SyncBatchNorm in distributed settings rather than relying on accumulation. LayerNorm doesn't have this issue because it normalizes per sample. Other catches: dropout patterns differ (independent across micro-batches vs whether a true batch-256 would have done something specific, though usually doesn't matter); learning rate scaling rules tied to batch size assume the gradient noise behavior of a true batch, which accumulation matches well; throughput is worse than a true large batch on the same hardware because you do the same FLOPs but with more sequential steps; and the wall-clock per optimizer update is higher, which can affect training time even when the effective batch is the same. Useful trick despite the catches; just know what it does and doesn't replicate.

expected_points.point: Accumulate gradients across micro-batches before optimizer step to simulate large effective batch.
Scale loss by 1/accum_steps to keep gradient magnitudes correct.
BatchNorm statistics are computed per micro-batch, so accumulation does not replicate large-batch BN behavior.
LayerNorm and similar per-sample norms are unaffected.
Wall-clock cost is the same FLOPs but slower steps; not free.

question_text: You have a budget to label 10,000 examples for a classification task. How do you decide which examples to label?
model_answer: Random sampling is a fine baseline but almost never the right answer when labels are expensive. The goal is to maximize the value of each label, which usually means labeling examples that are informative for the model. Several strategies, layered. First, ensure baseline coverage: stratified random sampling that ensures every class and every important slice (geography, language, customer segment) is represented. Without this, your model will be blind to underrepresented populations regardless of how clever the rest of your strategy is. Maybe 30% of budget. Second, active learning: train an initial model on whatever labels you have or a small seed set, then use it to score the unlabeled pool and prioritize labeling examples where the model is uncertain (high entropy on the predicted distribution) or where small ensembles disagree. The intuition: examples the model is confident about don't add information; examples it's confused about are decision-boundary cases. Maybe 40-50% of budget. Third, hard or rare examples: deliberately label examples from places your current model fails (false positives, false negatives from production logs), examples in long-tail regions of the input distribution, examples flagged by users as bad. These are the cases the model needs the most. Maybe 15-25% of budget. Fourth, watch for label quality, not just quantity: 10,000 noisy labels is often worse than 5,000 high-quality ones with double-labeling on disagreements. Build in quality checks, golden questions, inter-annotator agreement metrics. If agreement is below 0.7 kappa, your task definition is ambiguous and you need to fix that before labeling more. Fifth, plan for evaluation specifically: reserve 10-20% of the budget for a held-out test set that's labeled to a higher quality bar, with multi-annotator consensus. Your model is only as good as the eval set; underspending here is the most common mistake. Sixth, iterate: label in batches of 1-2K, retrain, re-prioritize with active learning, label the next batch. A single 10K label dump trained on once is far less effective than 5 batches of 2K with model improvement guiding selection. The meta-point: labeling strategy is a problem worth designing as carefully as the model itself, because the labels bound the achievable performance. Cheap labels in bulk are not a substitute for thoughtful selection.

expected_points.point: Stratified random sampling for baseline coverage across classes and segments.
Active learning to prioritize uncertain or boundary examples.
Target known model failures and rare/long-tail examples.
Invest in label quality (double-labeling, agreement metrics) as much as quantity.
Reserve high-quality budget for the evaluation set.
Iterate in batches with active learning between rounds.

question_text: You're running an LLM-powered application and 60% of requests have similar prompts. How do you design caching to reduce cost without hurting quality?
model_answer: There are several layers of caching for LLM apps, and they have different cost-benefit profiles. First, exact-match caching: hash the full prompt (including system prompt and any context) and cache the response. Cheap, easy, completely safe. Catches identical requests; useful for common queries like FAQ-style asks. Limitation: even tiny variations (a trailing space, a different greeting) miss the cache, so hit rate is low for natural-language traffic. Second, semantic caching: embed the prompt, look up similar prompts in a vector index, and if similarity exceeds a threshold, return the cached response. Hit rate is much higher because 'how do I reset my password' and 'reset password please' map to the same semantic neighborhood. The risk is that 'similar' isn't 'identical' in meaning; you can return a wrong answer for a question that looks similar but isn't. Mitigations: high similarity thresholds (0.95+), exclude queries that include user-specific details (names, IDs, recent context), restrict semantic caching to a curated set of safe query types, and validate periodically that cached responses still match if asked fresh. Third, prompt caching at the LLM layer: providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, and self-hosted vLLM support caching the KV state for a long shared prefix (system prompt, few-shot examples, retrieved documents). When the prefix is reused, you pay only for the new tokens. This is huge for RAG and agent systems where the system prompt and tool definitions are reused; can cut costs by 50-90% and reduce latency dramatically. Cheap to enable, no quality risk. Fourth, response streaming and partial caching: cache embeddings of common contexts so retrieval doesn't need to recompute, cache tool call results when arguments are deterministic. What I'd worry about. Cache invalidation: if your knowledge base updates, semantic cache results may be stale. TTLs and cache invalidation hooks per domain. Personalization: don't cache responses that depend on user state unless the cache key includes that state. Privacy: caching across users can leak information; a cache that returns 'last user's account balance was X' is a serious bug. Always include user identity in the cache key for anything user-scoped, or scope caches per tenant. Quality monitoring: log cache hit rate and periodically sample cached responses and compare to fresh generations; quality regression on the cached path is invisible without monitoring. Practical recommendation: start with prompt caching (lowest risk, highest leverage), add exact-match caching for common queries, and only deploy semantic caching after careful evaluation with your specific traffic.

expected_points.point: Exact-match caching: cheap, safe, low hit rate.
Semantic caching with embeddings: higher hit rate but quality risk; needs threshold tuning and constraints.
Prompt prefix caching at the LLM layer is the highest-leverage and lowest-risk lever.
Cache key must include user/tenant identity for personalized content; privacy risk.
TTL and invalidation strategy when knowledge updates.
Monitor cached vs fresh response quality to catch regressions.

question_text: A PM wants to use 'session duration' as the success metric for a content recommendation experiment. What concerns would you raise?
model_answer: Session duration is appealing because it's easy to measure, but it's a problematic primary metric for content recommendation. Several issues. First, it's not aligned with user welfare, only with engagement. Optimizing session duration can mean optimizing for content that keeps people scrolling against their better judgment, which is a known anti-pattern in social and media products. The user-friendly version of the goal is something like 'time well spent' or 'satisfaction-weighted engagement,' which is harder to measure but closer to what we actually want to maximize. Second, it confounds quality and frustration. A session that's long because the user couldn't find what they wanted, or because they had to scroll past bad recommendations to find good ones, looks identical to a session that's long because the user is enjoying themselves. Without complementary signals (explicit ratings, return visits, content shares), you can't distinguish. Third, it can be gamed unintentionally by the model. The optimizer will find ways to extend sessions that have nothing to do with recommendation quality: autoplay tricks, infinite scroll designs, content that's mildly addictive but not satisfying. The model is doing exactly what you asked, but you asked the wrong question. Fourth, it has heavy variance and seasonality, which makes A/B tests underpowered or noisy. Fifth, it doesn't capture downstream effects. A change that increases this-session duration but reduces tomorrow's return rate is a net loss, and short-window metrics miss this. The constructive ask: what does the PM actually want? If it's 'users engage with our content,' there are better metrics: meaningful interactions per session (likes, shares, saves), retention at D7/D30, satisfaction surveys, content completion rate (videos watched to end, articles read past the fold). For experiments, I'd push for a primary metric tied to longer-term engagement, with session duration as a guardrail. The framing for the PM: 'the metric you optimize, you get more of, including the parts you didn't mean,' so picking the right metric is the most important design choice in the experiment. Goodhart's law isn't an academic concern, it's the most reliable failure mode in product analytics.

expected_points.point: Session duration is engagement, not satisfaction; can incentivize anti-user patterns.
Confounds quality with frustration; long sessions can mean either.
Goodhart's law: optimizing the metric makes it less meaningful as a measure.
Misses long-term effects: high session duration today vs return rate tomorrow.
Suggest better metrics: retention, meaningful actions, completion, satisfaction.
Use suspect metrics as guardrails, not primary; primary should reflect user value.

question_text: You have a fixed compute budget for pretraining a language model. Walk me through how you'd decide model size and training tokens.
model_answer: This is the question scaling laws were invented to answer, and the answer has shifted over time. The Kaplan et al. 2020 paper said: for a fixed compute budget, you should mostly scale up model size and not train on too much data; the optimum was something like 80% of compute on bigger models, 20% on more tokens. That guidance was wrong because of an issue with how the experiments were set up. Hoffmann et al. 2022 (the Chinchilla paper) revisited this and showed that compute-optimal training requires roughly 20 tokens per parameter, meaning a 1B parameter model wants about 20B training tokens, a 70B model wants 1.4T tokens. The implication was that most existing models, including GPT-3 at 175B trained on ~300B tokens, were significantly under-trained for their parameter count, and Chinchilla at 70B trained on 1.4T tokens beat them while being much cheaper to serve. So how I'd actually decide. Step one, estimate compute budget in FLOPs. Roughly, training FLOPs is approximately 6 * N * D, where N is parameters and D is training tokens. If you have C FLOPs, you're picking N and D such that 6 * N * D ≤ C. Step two, apply the Chinchilla scaling: optimal D/N ratio of around 20. So given C, set N = sqrt(C / (6 * 20)) and D = 20 * N. Step three, adjust for inference cost. Chinchilla optimal is for training compute, but if the model will be served heavily, training a smaller model on more tokens than Chinchilla suggests is often economically right. Llama models and most production models go significantly past Chinchilla optimal because inference dominates total cost. The Llama 3 8B was trained on 15 trillion tokens, which is something like 1875 tokens per parameter, far past Chinchilla. The model gets better, training is somewhat less compute-efficient, but inference is much cheaper per query. Step four, data quality and availability constrain things. You can't just demand more tokens if you don't have high-quality ones; chinchilla scaling assumes data quality is held constant. Multi-epoch training on a smaller corpus can substitute partially but with diminishing returns and overfitting risk. Step five, reserve budget for hyperparameter search and instruction tuning afterward; the pretraining run isn't the whole story. Practical recommendation today: target somewhere between Chinchilla optimal and 5-10x past it, biased toward more tokens for production models, and validate on a smaller scale first because scaling laws are only directionally accurate.

expected_points.point: Approximate training compute as 6*N*D for parameters N and tokens D.
Chinchilla finding: roughly 20 tokens per parameter is compute-optimal for training.
Critique earlier Kaplan scaling laws as having underestimated optimal data.
Inference cost considerations push past Chinchilla optimal in production.
Data quality and availability are real constraints not captured by simple scaling laws.
Validate at small scale; scaling laws are directional.

question_text: You have a Python loop computing pairwise distances between two arrays of 10K vectors each. It takes 30 minutes. Make it fast.
model_answer:
30 minutes for 100M pairwise distances is the classic Python interpreter overhead, not an algorithm problem. The fix is vectorization. Naive code: ```python
distances = []
for a in A:
    row = []
    for b in B:
        row.append(np.linalg.norm(a - b))
    distances.append(row)
```
This evaluates 100M Python-level operations, each of which calls into NumPy with overhead. Vectorized version: ```python
# Broadcasting: A is (N,D), B is (M,D)
diff = A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :]  # (N, M, D)
distances = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=-1)  # (N, M)
```
This runs in seconds instead of minutes because NumPy does the entire computation in compiled C code with no Python loop overhead. For Euclidean distance specifically, the even faster trick exploits ||a - b||^2 = ||a||^2 + ||b||^2 - 2*a.b: ```python
A_sq = (A**2).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)  # (N, 1)
B_sq = (B**2).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True).T  # (1, M)
distances = np.sqrt(A_sq + B_sq - 2 * A @ B.T)
```
This is fastest because matrix multiplication is the most optimized operation in any numerical library. For very large arrays, the broadcasting version allocates an (N, M, D) intermediate which can blow up memory; the matmul version only needs (N, M). Even better for production: use scipy.spatial.distance.cdist or sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances which handle edge cases and dispatch to BLAS. For massive scale (millions of vectors), you'd use FAISS for approximate nearest neighbor instead of computing the full distance matrix at all. The lesson: vectorize first, optimize second. The Python loop overhead is almost always the dominant cost in 'slow numpy code,' and rewriting to broadcast or matmul typically wins 100-1000x without any algorithmic change.

expected_points.point: Identify the issue as Python loop overhead, not algorithmic complexity.
Use broadcasting to compute the full distance matrix in one NumPy call.
Apply the ||a-b||^2 expansion to use matmul, the most optimized op.
Note memory tradeoff: broadcasting allocates large intermediate, matmul version doesn't.
For production, use scipy/sklearn or FAISS rather than reimplementing.

question_text: How would you set up model versioning and rollback for a team that ships ML model updates weekly?
model_answer: Weekly cadence means you need infrastructure, not heroics. The components I'd put in place. First, a model registry with strict semantic versioning: every model has a unique ID, a version, the training data hash, the code commit hash, the hyperparameters, and the evaluation metrics on a fixed holdout. This is non-negotiable; without it you can't reason about what's deployed. Use a tool like MLflow, Weights & Biases, or a simple internal registry; the tool matters less than the discipline. Second, immutability: once a model is registered, it's frozen. Re-running the training pipeline produces a new version, never modifies the old one. This is what makes rollback meaningful. Third, deployment pinning: production references a specific model version, not 'latest.' The deployment config (whether it's a Kubernetes manifest, a feature flag, or a serving config) explicitly names the version. Promoting a new version is a config change, reviewed and audited, not a model upload. Fourth, automated evaluation gate: before any version reaches production, it must pass an evaluation suite that includes the previous champion's eval set plus regression tests on important slices (high-stakes customer segments, edge cases discovered in past incidents). A model that beats overall metrics but regresses on a critical slice is blocked. Fifth, deployment strategy: every version goes through shadow then canary then full rollout, with automated rollback if guardrail metrics breach thresholds. The rollback is itself a config change to the previous version, takes seconds, and triggers an alert and post-mortem. Sixth, monitoring tied to model version: every prediction is logged with the model version that made it, so when something goes wrong you can attribute it to a specific version and diff against the previous one. Seventh, training-serving parity: the same feature pipeline code runs in training and serving, and you periodically run consistency tests where you score the same input through both paths and assert equality. This catches a class of subtle bugs that otherwise present as 'the new model is mysteriously bad in production.' Eighth, documentation and changelog: every promoted version has a one-paragraph description of what changed and why; this is what you'll wish you had at 2 AM during an incident six months later. Ninth, decommissioning policy: old versions should be eventually removable, but keep at least the last 3-5 in cold storage so rollback to anything within recent history is possible. Tenth, a deployment review process: a single human signs off on production promotions, even if the gate is automated. The point isn't to gate-keep, it's to ensure someone is responsible. The cultural piece matters as much as the tooling: rollbacks should be celebrated, not punished. A team that rolls back fast and learns is much safer than a team that ships slowly out of fear.

expected_points.point: Model registry with full lineage: data hash, code commit, hyperparameters, metrics.
Immutability of registered versions; new training produces new version.
Deployment pinning to specific versions, not 'latest'; promotion is reviewed config change.
Automated evaluation gates including slice-level regressions before promotion.
Shadow/canary/full rollout with automated rollback on guardrail breach.
Per-prediction model version logging for attribution; training-serving parity tests.

question_text: For a tabular classification problem with 200K rows and 80 features, why is gradient boosting still the default, and when would you switch to a neural network?
model_answer: On tabular data of this scale, XGBoost or LightGBM is the default for several reasons that have held up despite years of neural network research trying to dethrone them. First, they handle the actual structure of tabular data well: heterogeneous feature types, missing values natively (especially LightGBM with its missing-value-aware splits), feature interactions discovered automatically through tree splits, robustness to feature scaling, and scale invariance per feature. A neural network needs all this to be engineered manually. Second, they're sample-efficient. With 200K rows, gradient boosting often hits its asymptotic performance; a neural network typically needs an order of magnitude more data to match it on tabular tasks. Third, they're fast to train, easy to tune (a handful of hyperparameters that don't interact wildly), and produce well-calibrated probabilities with sigmoid output and binary log-loss. Fourth, the tooling is mature: feature importance, SHAP values, monotonic constraints, cross-validation are all first-class. Fifth, the academic record: papers like 'Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?' (2022) show that on standard benchmarks, gradient boosting wins reliably across dozens of datasets. When would I switch to a neural network? Several scenarios. First, when you have very high cardinality categorical features that benefit from learned embeddings, like user IDs, product IDs, geographic codes. Trees with target encoding or hashing handle this poorly; embeddings learn a useful representation. Second, when you have unstructured features mixed with tabular: text descriptions, images, sequences. A neural network lets you process those with appropriate sub-networks (text encoder, CNN, etc.) and combine them with tabular features in one model. Trees can use embeddings as features but can't learn them. Third, when there's significant temporal structure (sequences of user actions) or relational structure (graph neighborhoods); transformers or GNNs encode that naturally. Fourth, at very large scale with rich data, where the neural network's capacity for representation learning starts to pay off. Fifth, when you need a multi-task setup with shared parameters across related tasks; trees don't share parameters. Sixth, when downstream uses require differentiable predictions, like in a larger end-to-end system. Otherwise, my default is XGBoost or LightGBM, with a neural baseline I check against. The honest framing: 'use the boring thing that works' is correct surprisingly often.

expected_points.point: Trees handle heterogeneous features, missing values, and scale invariance natively.
Sample efficiency on tabular data: gradient boosting hits asymptote at modest data sizes.
Mature tooling: SHAP, monotonic constraints, calibration.
Switch to NN for high-cardinality categoricals benefiting from embeddings.
Neural nets for mixed unstructured features (text, image) or sequence/graph structure.
Acknowledge the academic record showing trees still win on most tabular benchmarks.

question_text: Train loss is 0.05, validation loss is 0.50. Then you double the training data and now train loss is 0.20, validation loss is 0.30. What happened and what does it suggest?
model_answer: The first regime (0.05 train, 0.50 val) is classic overfitting: large gap between train and val, train loss is very low, model memorized the training set. The second regime (0.20 train, 0.30 val) shows the gap closed but train loss went up; the model can no longer memorize the larger training set, and val loss improved. So adding data helped, which is informative: it tells you the model has enough capacity (or even excess), and the bottleneck was data. Several conclusions follow. First, more data continues to be a high-leverage lever; if you can get even more, you'll likely improve further. The marginal value of data hasn't run out. Second, you might still have headroom on capacity. Train loss went up because the model can't fit the larger set as easily; this could mean it's now underfitting slightly. If you add a bit more capacity (more parameters, longer training), you might push both losses down further while maintaining the closed gap. Third, the regularization choice should be revisited. With a smaller dataset, heavy regularization was probably needed to control the gap. With more data, you can afford less regularization, which lets the model fit better. Concretely: lower weight decay, less dropout, less aggressive data augmentation. Fourth, this is the canonical 'are we capacity-bound or data-bound' diagnostic, and the answer here is that we were data-bound. The next experiments to run: scale data further to estimate the data scaling curve; scale capacity to find the new sweet spot; ablate regularization. The general rule of thumb: when train and val losses are similar and high, you're underfitting (more capacity, less regularization, or more features); when train is low and val is high, you're overfitting (more data, more regularization, simpler model); when both are low, you're probably done unless you can get more data and a bigger model. The transition between regimes as you change data is the most informative experiment, often more so than any single training run.

expected_points.point: First regime is overfitting: large train-val gap, low train loss.
Second regime: gap closed, train loss rose, val improved; data helped.
Conclude the model was data-bound; more data likely continues to help.
Reduce regularization now that the gap has closed; may add capacity.
Frame as the standard underfit/overfit diagnostic and what each regime implies.

question_text: An LLM provider releases a 1M-token context window. Should you stop using RAG?
model_answer: No, but the calculus does shift. Long context is a powerful capability, not a replacement for retrieval. Several reasons. First, cost. Even with KV caching, putting a million tokens in context per request is expensive at any non-trivial query volume. RAG retrieves a few thousand relevant tokens per query; long context loads the entire corpus every time. The math doesn't favor long context for any production workload that scales beyond demos. Second, attention quality at long context isn't what marketing materials suggest. The 'needle in a haystack' benchmark, where you put a single fact at random positions and ask the model to retrieve it, is a degenerate test that most modern long-context models pass. Real long-context tasks (multi-document reasoning, attention to specific subsections among similar ones, integration of information across distant parts of the context) show much steeper degradation. Lost-in-the-middle effects, where information in the middle of a long context is poorly utilized, are documented across multiple models and benchmarks. Third, freshness. RAG retrieves from an index that you can update incrementally; long-context loads the document set you've decided on at query time. If your knowledge base updates daily, you don't want to re-tokenize and re-prefill the same documents on every query. Fourth, attribution and traceability. RAG returns citations naturally because you know which documents were retrieved; with long context, the model has 'seen everything' and citations become a generation task that's prone to hallucination. For regulated or audit-sensitive applications, RAG's transparency is a feature. Fifth, security and access control. RAG can apply per-user access controls at the retrieval layer (don't return documents this user shouldn't see); long context tends toward 'load everything,' which is a security and privacy nightmare in multi-tenant or regulated settings. When does long context win? When the task genuinely needs reasoning across the whole document set, like 'summarize all changes across these 200 PDFs' or 'find inconsistencies between these contracts.' Or when the corpus is small and queries are infrequent (a single-user research assistant for a personal document set). Or as a complement to RAG: retrieve more permissively (top-100 instead of top-5) and let the model use its long context to filter and reason. The right framing: long context expands the design space rather than collapsing it. Use both, and pick the right tool per task.

expected_points.point: Cost comparison: RAG retrieves thousands of tokens, long context loads entire corpus per query.
Long-context attention quality degrades on realistic tasks beyond needle-in-haystack.
RAG supports incremental index updates; long context requires re-loading.
RAG provides natural citations and attribution; long context citations are generated.
Access control and security favor retrieval-layer filtering.
Long context complements rather than replaces RAG; can retrieve more broadly and reason in context.
